subject: science
title: Science Book — Elevate Science, Course 1 (Grade 6)
intro: Follow along with your Elevate Science textbook — every chapter and lesson, in order, with short videos to help each idea click!

lessons.title: Describing and Classifying Matter
lessons.teach: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space — your desk, the air, and you are all matter. Scientists describe matter by its physical properties (things you can observe without changing it, like color, hardness, and melting point) and its chemical properties (how it reacts to form new substances, like rusting or burning). A pure substance is made of only one kind of matter, while a mixture is two or more substances mixed together but not chemically joined.

lessons.title: Measuring Matter
lessons.teach: To measure matter, scientists use mass (how much matter an object contains, measured in grams) and volume (how much space it takes up, measured in milliliters or cubic centimeters). Density tells you how tightly matter is packed — it is mass divided by volume. Two objects can be the same size but have different densities; that's why a small rock sinks but a big beach ball floats.

lessons.title: Changes in Matter
lessons.teach: Matter can change in two main ways. In a physical change, the matter looks different but is still the same substance — like ice melting into water or paper being torn. In a chemical change, the matter turns into a brand-new substance — like wood burning into ash or iron rusting. A big clue that a chemical change happened is a color change, bubbles, heat, or light that you can't easily undo.

lessons.title: States of Matter
lessons.teach: Matter usually comes in three states: solid, liquid, and gas. In a solid, particles are packed tightly and only vibrate in place, so it keeps its shape. In a liquid, particles are close but can slide past each other, so it flows and takes the shape of its container. In a gas, particles spread far apart and zoom around, so gas fills any space it's in.

lessons.title: Changes of State
lessons.teach: Matter can change from one state to another when it gains or loses thermal energy. Adding heat can melt a solid into a liquid or evaporate a liquid into a gas. Removing heat can condense a gas into a liquid or freeze a liquid into a solid. During these changes the substance stays the same — only its state changes as the particles speed up or slow down.

lessons.title: Gas Behavior
lessons.teach: Gases behave in special ways because their particles are far apart and move fast. The more you squeeze a gas into a smaller space, the higher its pressure climbs. Heating a gas makes its particles move faster and spread out, so the gas expands or pushes harder. These relationships between volume, temperature, and pressure explain why a balloon shrinks in the cold and grows in the heat.

lessons.title: What Is Energy?
lessons.teach: Energy is the ability to do work or cause change. Two important kinds are kinetic energy, the energy of motion that anything moving has, and potential energy, stored energy because of an object's position — like a ball at the top of a hill ready to roll. The more mass an object has and the faster it moves, the more kinetic energy it has.

lessons.title: Forms of Energy
lessons.teach: Energy comes in many forms. Mechanical energy is the energy of moving objects, thermal energy comes from moving particles and gives us heat, and chemical energy is stored in food, fuel, and batteries. There is also electrical energy, light energy, and sound energy. All these forms can do work and can be changed from one form into another.

lessons.title: Energy Transformations and Conservation
lessons.teach: Energy is constantly transformed, or changed, from one form into another — a flashlight turns chemical energy into light, and a roller coaster turns potential energy into kinetic energy as it speeds downhill. The Law of Conservation of Energy says energy is never created or destroyed; it only changes form. So the total amount of energy always stays the same.

lessons.title: Temperature, Thermal Energy, and Heat
lessons.teach: Temperature measures how fast the particles in matter are moving — faster particles mean a higher temperature. Thermal energy is the total energy of all those moving particles. Heat is thermal energy that flows from a warmer object to a cooler object. Heat always moves from hot to cold until both objects reach the same temperature.

lessons.title: Heat Transfer: Radiation, Conduction, Convection
lessons.teach: Heat moves in three ways. Radiation is heat traveling as rays through empty space — that's how the Sun's heat reaches Earth. Conduction is heat passing directly from one touching object to another, like a hot pan warming your hand. Convection is heat moving in flowing liquids or gases, where warm material rises and cool material sinks, creating circular currents in air, oceans, and even Earth's mantle.

lessons.title: Thermal Energy and Materials
lessons.teach: Different materials respond to heat differently. Conductors, like metals, let heat flow through them quickly, which is why a metal spoon gets hot in soup. Insulators, like wood, plastic, and air, slow heat down, which is why oven mitts protect your hands. Engineers choose conductors or insulators on purpose to control where heat goes.

lessons.title: Earth's Interior
lessons.teach: Earth is made of layers, like a giant ball with a hard shell and a hot center. The thin outer layer we live on is the crust. Below it is the thick, hot mantle, which is solid rock that can slowly flow over time. At the center is the core — a super-hot outer core of liquid metal and an inner core of solid metal. The deeper you go, the hotter and denser it gets.

lessons.title: Earth's Spheres Interacting
lessons.teach: Earth is made of connected systems called spheres. The geosphere is the solid rock and land, the hydrosphere is all the liquid water, the cryosphere is the frozen ice and snow, the atmosphere is the air around us, and the biosphere is all living things. These spheres constantly interact — for example, rain (hydrosphere) wears down mountains (geosphere) and gives water to plants (biosphere). Earth works as one big connected system.

lessons.title: Energy from the Sun
lessons.teach: The Sun is the main source of energy for almost everything on Earth. Because Earth is round, the Sun heats different places by different amounts — the equator gets the most direct sunlight, while the poles get less. This uneven heating makes air and water move, creating wind, ocean currents, and weather. Land, water, and air also heat up and cool down at different speeds, which adds to these patterns.

lessons.title: The Atmosphere and Water in the Air
lessons.teach: Earth's atmosphere is the blanket of gases surrounding the planet, and it does much more than give us air to breathe. It is layered, and the ozone in the upper atmosphere blocks harmful ultraviolet rays from the Sun. Water moves into the air through evaporation, then cools and condenses to form clouds, fog, and dew. Humidity is the amount of water vapor in the air.

lessons.title: The Water Cycle and Weather Patterns
lessons.teach: Water is constantly recycled between the ground, oceans, and sky in the water cycle. The Sun's heat causes evaporation, turning liquid water into invisible water vapor that rises. Up high the vapor cools and condenses into tiny droplets, forming clouds. When the droplets get heavy enough they fall as precipitation — rain, snow, or hail — and the water collects again to start the cycle over, shaping our weather and climate.

lessons.title: Air Masses, Fronts, and Predicting Weather
lessons.teach: Giant bodies of air called air masses can be warm or cold, wet or dry. Where two air masses meet, they form a boundary called a front, which often brings clouds, storms, and changing weather. Global patterns like the jet stream (a fast river of high-altitude wind) and ocean currents steer these weather systems. Meteorologists track temperature, air pressure, wind, and humidity to predict what's coming.

lessons.title: Severe Weather and Staying Safe in Florida
lessons.teach: Florida faces hazardous weather like hurricanes, lightning, flooding, and intense sun. These natural disasters can damage homes and threaten lives, so people prepare and protect themselves. To stay safe, Floridians track storms, evacuate when told, board up windows, and keep emergency supplies. For everyday sun safety, people use sunscreen, hats, and shade to block harmful ultraviolet rays.

topics.title: Topic 7 — Minerals and Rocks in the Geosphere

lessons.title: Minerals
lessons.teach: A mineral is a naturally formed solid with a specific chemical makeup and an orderly crystal pattern inside. Scientists identify minerals by their properties, such as color, hardness, luster (how shiny they are), and streak (the color of their powder). Minerals are the building blocks of rocks, and we use them in everything from pencils to phones.

lessons.title: Rocks and How They Form
lessons.teach: Rocks are made of one or more minerals and come in three main types. Igneous rock forms when melted rock cools and hardens. Sedimentary rock forms when bits of rock and sand get pressed and cemented together in layers. Metamorphic rock forms when heat and pressure change an existing rock without melting it. The type of rock tells a story about how and where it formed.

lessons.title: The Rock Cycle
lessons.teach: Rocks are always slowly changing from one type to another in a loop called the rock cycle. Heat and pressure can turn rock into metamorphic rock, melting can turn it into magma that cools into igneous rock, and weathering can break it into sediment that hardens into sedimentary rock. Over millions of years, any rock can become any other type as it melts, breaks down, or gets squeezed.

lessons.title: Drifting Continents
lessons.teach: Long ago, scientist Alfred Wegener noticed that the continents look like puzzle pieces that could fit together. He proposed the idea of continental drift — that all the continents were once joined in one giant supercontinent called Pangaea and have slowly drifted apart. Matching rocks, fossils, and mountain ranges on different continents became evidence that they were once connected.

lessons.title: Sea-Floor Spreading
lessons.teach: Deep under the oceans, hot melted rock rises up through long cracks called mid-ocean ridges. As it cools, it adds new rock to the sea floor and pushes the older sea floor outward on both sides. This process, called sea-floor spreading, gave scientists strong evidence for how Earth's surface moves and helped explain how continents drift apart.

lessons.title: The Theory of Plate Tectonics
lessons.teach: Earth's crust is broken into giant pieces called tectonic plates that slowly float on the soft mantle below. These plates move just a few centimeters a year, but over millions of years they push together, pull apart, or slide past each other. Where plates meet, they build mountains, open oceans, and cause earthquakes and volcanoes. This is why Earth's surface is always slowly changing.

lessons.title: Weathering and Soil
lessons.teach: Weathering is when rock is broken into smaller pieces. Mechanical weathering breaks rock apart physically, like ice cracking it or roots pushing through it, while chemical weathering dissolves or changes the rock with water and acids. Over a very long time, weathered rock mixes with dead plant and animal matter to form soil, which living things depend on.

lessons.title: Erosion and Deposition
lessons.teach: Erosion is when broken pieces of rock and soil get carried away by wind, water, ice, or gravity. Deposition is when those pieces finally get dropped in a new place, building up land like sandbars, beaches, and deltas. Together, weathering, erosion, and deposition form a never-ending cycle that constantly reshapes Earth's surface.

lessons.title: Landforms (and Florida's Landforms)
lessons.teach: A landform is a natural feature of Earth's surface, such as mountains, rivers, coastlines, dunes, glaciers, deltas, and lakes. Different forces create different landforms — rivers carve valleys, while waves and wind shape sandy coastlines and dunes. Florida is mostly flat and low, with long sandy coastlines, beaches, dunes, wetlands like the Everglades, and many lakes, but no real mountains or glaciers.

topics.title: Topic 10 — Living Things in the Biosphere

lessons.title: What Are Living Things?
lessons.teach: Living things, or organisms, share certain features: they are made of cells, use energy, grow and develop, respond to their surroundings, and reproduce. The cell is the basic building block of all living things — some organisms are made of just one cell, while others, like you, are made of trillions. Scientists organize life from atoms and molecules up to cells, tissues, organs, and whole organisms.

lessons.title: Classifying Living Things
lessons.teach: There are millions of kinds of living things, so scientists classify, or group, them by shared characteristics. This makes organisms easier to study and compare. Scientists use the Linnaean system together with broad groups called domains to sort all life. Each organism gets a two-part scientific name so people everywhere know exactly which living thing they mean.

lessons.title: Energy and Matter in Ecosystems
lessons.teach: An ecosystem is all the living and nonliving things in an area working together. Energy enters most ecosystems from the Sun: plants capture sunlight to make food, then animals eat the plants, and other animals eat those animals. This flow of energy from one living thing to the next is shown by food chains and food webs. Matter, like water and nutrients, gets recycled and used again and again.

lessons.title: Microorganisms: Viruses, Bacteria, Protists, and Fungi
lessons.teach: Some living things are too small to see without a microscope. Bacteria are tiny single-celled organisms found almost everywhere, some helpful and some harmful. Protists and fungi are other groups of organisms, like algae, amoebas, and mushrooms. Viruses are even smaller and are not quite alive — they can only reproduce by invading a living cell. Comparing these tiny agents helps us understand health and disease.
